mainTopic: How דוד died on שבת and putting out a lamp for a sick person; why קהלת and משלי were nearly hidden; joy and the שכינה; answering fools; patience like הלל
overview: This amud finishes the story of how דוד המלך died on שבת, and of how שלמה asked the בית המדרש what to do with his father's body and the hungry dogs. These stories complete רב תנחום's answer: one may put out a lamp on שבת for a sick person, because a person's soul is God's 'lamp'. The talk of contradictions in קהלת leads to רב's teaching that חכמים wanted to hide ספר קהלת, but it was kept because it begins and ends with דברי תורה. The גמרא then resolves its contradictions about laughter and joy, and teaches that the שכינה rests only on a person who is in שמחה של מצוה. This leads to a discussion of whether a teacher of הלכה should be joyful or in awe, and רבה's practice shows how both fit. ספר משלי was also nearly hidden, because one verse says to answer a fool and the next says not to. The answer is that one ignores a fool in everyday matters, as the stories of רבי and רבי חייא show. One does answer a fool in דברי תורה, as רבן גמליאל did with a mocking student. The amud ends with a ברייתא praising the patience of הלל over the strictness of שמאי, whose first story continues on the next amud.

steps.title: דוד learned all שבת, so מלאך המות could not take him
steps.stepSummary: דוד המלך learned without stopping every שבת, so מלאך המות could not take him on the day he was meant to die.
steps.simpleTranslation: Every שבת דוד would sit and learn the whole day. On the day he was supposed to die, מלאך המות stood in front of him but could not overpower him, because his mouth never stopped learning.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the story of how דוד המלך died. Because he was always learning on שבת, מלאך המות could not get to him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, דוד was told he would die on a שבת. So he learned all day every שבת. The idea is that תורה learning protects a person from death while he is doing it. This sets up the trick מלאך המות uses next.

keyTerms.meaning: for his soul to rest (to die)

phrases.english: Every Shabbat day
he would sit and learn the whole day.
On that day when his soul was supposed to come to rest,
the Angel of Death stood before him
and could not overpower him,
because his mouth did not stop from learning.

steps.triggerLanguage: כׇּל יוֹמָא דְשַׁבְּתָא הֲוָה יָתֵיב וְגָרֵיס כּוּלֵּי יוֹמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the David story begun on the previous amud.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תורה learning shielded דוד from מלאך המות.

steps.title: מלאך המות distracts דוד and he dies
steps.stepSummary: מלאך המות shakes the trees in דוד's garden. דוד goes out to look, the stair breaks, he stops learning for a moment, and he dies.
steps.simpleTranslation: מלאך המות said: What can I do to him? דוד had a garden behind his house. מלאך המות went and climbed up and shook the trees. דוד went out to see. As he climbed the stairs, the stair broke under him. He went quiet, and he died.
steps.whatsHappening: מלאך המות makes a noise in the garden to distract דוד. In the one moment דוד stops learning, he dies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Death could only come once the learning stopped. The important detail is that דוד died outside in the garden on שבת. This is what causes שלמה's question in the next step.

phrases.english: He (the Angel of Death) said: What shall I do to him?
He had a garden behind his house;

phrases.aramaic: אֲתָא מַלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת סָלֵיק וּבָחֵישׁ בְּאִילָנֵי.
phrases.english: the Angel of Death came, climbed up, and shook the trees.
He (David) went out to see.
As he was climbing the stair,
the stair broke beneath him;
he went silent, and his soul came to rest.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the story of דוד's death.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: דוד died in his garden on שבת during a pause in his learning.

steps.title: שלמה asks the בית המדרש what to do on שבת
steps.stepSummary: שלמה asks the בית המדרש what to do. His father's body is lying in the sun, and the household dogs are hungry.
steps.simpleTranslation: שלמה sent a question to the בית המדרש: My father died and is lying in the sun, and the dogs of my father's house are hungry. What should I do?
steps.whatsHappening: שלמה asks a practical שבת question with two parts. What can be done about the body in the sun, and what can be done about the hungry dogs?
steps.deeperAnalysis: A dead body is מוקצה and normally may not be moved on שבת. An animal carcass is also a moving problem. Leaving the body in the sun is disgraceful, and the hungry dogs might harm it.

phrases.english: Solomon sent to the study hall:
Father died and is lying in the sun,
and the dogs of father's house are hungry —
what shall I do?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The circumstances of דוד's death lead to a halachic question.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How to protect the body and feed the dogs without breaking the laws of moving things on שבת.

steps.title: Feed the dogs, and move the body using a loaf or a baby
steps.stepSummary: The בית המדרש answers: cut up a נבלה for the dogs, and move דוד's body by placing a loaf of bread or a baby on it.
steps.simpleTranslation: They sent back to him: Cut up an animal carcass and put it in front of the dogs. As for your father, put a loaf of bread or a baby on him, and then move him.
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים give שלמה two different rulings. The dogs may be fed directly, but דוד's body may only be moved through a trick.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Feeding living creatures is allowed, so the carcass may be handled for the dogs. A dead body may not be moved directly. But if a permitted object, like bread or a baby, is placed on it, the body may be moved together with it. The answer shows that a living dog's needs get a direct allowance, while the body of דוד המלך does not.

keyTerms.meaning: move it (טלטול, carrying or moving on שבת)

phrases.english: They sent to him:
Cut up a carcass and place it before the dogs.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָבִיךְ, הַנַּח עָלָיו כִּכָּר אוֹ תִּינוֹק
phrases.english: And your father — place a loaf or an infant on him
and move him.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלַחוּ לֵיהּ: חֲתוֹךְ נְבֵלָה וְהַנַּח לִפְנֵי הַכְּלָבִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers שלמה's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The carcass may be handled directly for the dogs. The body may be moved only by placing a loaf or a baby on it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This contrast becomes the proof in the next step that the living come before the dead.

steps.title: A living dog is better than a dead lion
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that שלמה spoke well when he said a living dog is better than a dead lion. This settles the contradiction about the living and the dead in קהלת.
steps.simpleTranslation: And didn't שלמה speak well when he said: 'For a living dog is better than a dead lion'?
steps.whatsHappening: The story is used to prove that life is more valuable than death. The hungry dogs got a more direct allowance than the body of דוד המלך.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, רב תנחום pointed out two verses in קהלת that seem to contradict each other. One praises the dead, and the other says a living dog is better than a dead lion. The שבת rulings show that the living dog really does come first. So the verse that values life is the one that holds.

keyTerms.meaning: and did he not speak well?

steps.whatToRemember: The halacha treats a living animal's needs more leniently than a dead king's body. So life comes before death.

phrases.english: And did Solomon not speak well:
"For a living dog is better
than the dead lion."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the lesson from the halachic answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Life is more valuable than death, as the verse 'a living dog is better than a dead lion' says.

steps.title: One may put out a lamp for a sick person
steps.stepSummary: רב תנחום answers the original question. A person's soul is called a 'נר', so a physical lamp may be put out to save God's lamp, the soul.
steps.simpleTranslation: And as for the question that I asked before you (רב תנחום says it modestly, since really they had asked him): A lamp is called 'נר', and a person's soul is called 'נר'. It is better that the lamp of a human being be put out for the sake of the lamp of הקדוש ברוך הוא.
steps.whatsHappening: רב תנחום comes back to the question he was actually asked: may one put out a lamp on שבת for a sick person? He answers yes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The source is the verse 'the spirit of man is the lamp of ה׳‎' (משלי). A man-made lamp is less important than a human soul. So putting out the lamp is allowed when it protects a sick person's life.
steps.whatToRemember: Final answer: one may put out a lamp on שבת for a sick person, because the human soul is God's 'lamp'.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two 'lamps'. The 'lamp of flesh and blood' is the physical lamp that people make. The 'lamp of הקדוש ברוך הוא' is the person's soul.

phrases.english: And regarding the question that I asked before you:
A lamp is called "ner,"
and a person's soul is called "ner."

phrases.aramaic: מוּטָב תִּכְבֶּה נֵר שֶׁל בָּשָׂר וָדָם
phrases.english: Better that the lamp of flesh and blood be extinguished

phrases.aramaic: מִפְּנֵי נֵרוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא.
phrases.english: for the sake of the lamp of the Holy One, Blessed be He.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns from the קהלת discussion to the original halachic question.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Putting out a lamp on שבת for a sick person is allowed.

steps.title: חכמים wanted to hide ספר קהלת
steps.stepSummary: In the name of רב: חכמים wanted to hide ספר קהלת, because its statements contradict each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה, son of רב שמואל בר שילת, said in the name of רב: חכמים wanted to hide away ספר קהלת, because its words contradict each other.
steps.whatsHappening: Since contradictions in קהלת just came up, the גמרא brings a related teaching. חכמים once wanted to put ספר קהלת away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To 'hide' a book means to take it out of public use so it will not confuse readers. The reason given is that it seems to contradict itself. This opens a new topic about קהלת.

keyTerms.meaning: to hide away or put out of use

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר שִׁילַת מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב:
phrases.english: Rav Yehuda son of Rav Shmuel bar Sheilat said in the name of Rav:
The Sages sought to hide away the book of Kohelet

phrases.aramaic: מִפְּנֵי שֶׁדְּבָרָיו סוֹתְרִין זֶה אֶת זֶה.
phrases.english: because its words contradict each other.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Linked by association: contradictions in קהלת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: חכמים considered hiding קהלת because of its internal contradictions.

steps.title: Why did they not hide it?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why, in the end, קהלת was not hidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why did they not hide it?
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup question. The גמרא is about to explain what saved קהלת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since there was a real reason to hide the book, there must have been a stronger reason to keep it.

phrases.english: And why did they not hide it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on רב's statement.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason קהלת was kept in the canon.

steps.title: It begins and ends with Torah
steps.stepSummary: קהלת was kept because both its beginning and its end are words of תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because its beginning is דברי תורה and its end is דברי תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the opening and the closing of קהלת are pure תורה. That saved the book.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The frame of the book shows its true message. The confusing middle parts must be read in light of that frame. The next two steps prove each half of this claim.

phrases.english: Because its beginning is words of Torah
and its end is words of Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The book opens and closes with words of תורה.

steps.title: Proof that the beginning is Torah
steps.stepSummary: The first verse says there is no gain 'under the sun'. The school of רבי ינאי reads this to mean there is gain 'before the sun', which means תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Its beginning is דברי תורה, as it is written: 'What profit does a person have from all his labor that he labors under the sun?' And the school of רבי ינאי said: Under the sun he has no profit, but before the sun he does.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves that the opening verse of קהלת is a תורה message. It does this through a close reading of the words 'under the sun'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Work 'under the sun' means worldly work, and it brings no lasting gain. תורה existed before the sun was created, so effort in תורה does bring real gain. What sounds like a gloomy verse is really praise of תורה.

keyTerms.meaning: before the sun (תורה, which came before creation)

phrases.english: Its beginning is words of Torah, as it is written:
"What profit has man from all his labor
that he labors under the sun?"
and the school of Rabbi Yannai said:
It is under the sun that he has no profit;
before the sun — he has.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proves the first half of the answer.
steps.raayaObject: That the opening of קהלת is words of תורה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: קהלת 1:3 as read by the school of רבי ינאי.

steps.title: Proof that the end is Torah
steps.stepSummary: The closing verse of קהלת commands fear of God and keeping His מצוות.
steps.simpleTranslation: Its end is דברי תורה, as it is written: 'The end of the matter, after all has been heard: Fear God and keep His commandments, for this is the whole person.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves the second half of the answer. The last verse of קהלת is plainly a תורה message.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike the first verse, this one needs no special reading, because it openly commands יראת שמים and keeping the מצוות. Its last phrase, 'this is the whole person', leads to the next question.

phrases.english: Its end is words of Torah, as it is written:
"The end of the matter, all having been heard:

phrases.aramaic: אֶת הָאֱלֹהִים יְרָא וְאֶת מִצְוֹתָיו שְׁמוֹר
phrases.english: Fear God and keep His commandments,
for this is the whole man."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proves the second half of the answer.
steps.raayaObject: That the end of קהלת is words of תורה.

steps.title: What does 'this is the whole man' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא stops to ask what the phrase 'for this is the whole man' means.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'for this is the whole man' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: This is a side question about the wording of the verse. It sets up three different explanations.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase is unclear. Does 'this' mean the God-fearing person, or something else? Three opinions follow.

phrases.english: What is "for this is the whole man"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the verse just quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of 'this is the whole man'.

steps.title: The world was created for the God-fearing person
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר says the whole world was created only for the sake of this God-fearing person.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: The entire world was created only for the sake of this person.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the first explanation of the phrase. The God-fearing person is the purpose of all creation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'This is the whole man' means that the person who fears God and keeps מצוות is what the whole world exists for.

keyTerms.meaning: for the sake of this one

steps.confusionAlert: The text shows a correction: (אליעזר) was replaced with [אלעזר]. The correct name is רבי אלעזר.

phrases.english: Rabbi (Eliezer) [Elazar] said:
phrases.notes: Some versions have the name in round brackets, אליעזר, but the corrected wording is the name in square brackets: רבי אלעזר.

phrases.english: The entire world was not created
except for the sake of this one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: First answer.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The world exists for the God-fearing person.

steps.title: This person equals the whole world
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא בר כהנא says the God-fearing person is equal in worth to the entire world.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא בר כהנא said: This person is equal to the entire world.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a second explanation. It is about the person's value, not about the purpose of creation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר said the world exists for this person. רבי אבא בר כהנא says this person is worth as much as the whole world, as if he were a world of his own.

phrases.english: Rabbi Abba bar Kahana said:

phrases.aramaic: שָׁקוּל זֶה כְּנֶגֶד כׇּל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ.
phrases.english: This one is equal to the entire world.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: An alternative to רבי אלעזר.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The God-fearing person equals the whole world in worth.

steps.title: The world was created as company for this person
steps.stepSummary: שמעון בן עזאי (some say שמעון בן זומא) says the whole world was created to keep this person company.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמעון בן עזאי says, and some say שמעון בן זומא says: The entire world was created only to be a companion to this person.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a third explanation, and the name of the speaker is reported in two versions. Creation serves as company for the God-fearing person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'לצוות' here means 'to accompany', not 'to command'. All of creation exists so that this person will not be alone.

keyTerms.meaning: to accompany or be a companion

steps.confusionAlert: Do not translate לצוות as 'to command'. Here it comes from צוותא, which means 'company'.
steps.whatToRemember: There are three readings of 'this is the whole man': the world was made for him, he equals the world, or the world was made to keep him company.

phrases.english: Shimon ben Azzai says,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן זוֹמָא אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: and some say Shimon ben Zoma says:
The entire world was not created
except as a companion to this one.

steps.triggerLanguage: שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן עַזַּאי אוֹמֵר, וְאָמְרִי לַהּ שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן זוֹמָא אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third alternative.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The world was created as company for the God-fearing person.

steps.title: The contradictions in קהלת are listed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows the contradictions. 'Anger is better than laughter' clashes with 'I said of laughter: it is praiseworthy'. 'I praised joy' clashes with 'of joy, what does it accomplish?'
steps.simpleTranslation: What are the contradicting words? It is written: 'Anger is better than laughter', and it is written: 'I said of laughter: it is praiseworthy'! It is written: 'I praised joy', and it is written: 'And of joy, what does it accomplish?'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to רב's statement. It spells out the contradictions that made חכמים want to hide קהלת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two pairs of verses. One pair is about laughter, and the other is about joy. In each pair, one verse praises the thing and the other puts it down.

phrases.english: And what is "its words contradict each other"?
It is written: "Anger is better than laughter,"
and it is written: "Of laughter I said: it is praiseworthy"!
It is written: "And I praised joy,"
and it is written: "And of joy, what does it accomplish?"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to רב's claim about contradictions.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Verses in the same book both praise and dismiss laughter and joy.

steps.title: Resolving the contradiction about laughter
steps.stepSummary: The two verses about laughter speak about different situations. God's anger at the righteous in this world is better than His 'laughter' with the wicked in this world. The praiseworthy laughter is God's laughter with the righteous in עולם הבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. 'Anger is better than laughter' means: The anger that God has toward the righteous in this world is better than the laughter God laughs with the wicked in this world. And 'Of laughter I said: it is praiseworthy' is the laughter God laughs with the righteous in עולם הבא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the first contradiction. Each verse is talking about a different kind of 'laughter'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this world, God may make things hard for צדיקים (anger), which is better than giving רשעים good things now (laughter). The praised laughter is the joy God shares with צדיקים in עולם הבא. So the two verses do not clash.

keyTerms.meaning: it is not difficult (the problem is resolved)

steps.confusionAlert: This step only answers the laughter contradiction. The joy (שמחה) contradiction is answered next.

phrases.english: It is not difficult: "Anger is better than laughter" means:

phrases.aramaic: טוֹב כַּעַס שֶׁכּוֹעֵס הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
phrases.english: Better is the anger with which the Holy One, Blessed be He, is angry
at the righteous in this world,
than the laughter that the Holy One, Blessed be He, laughs
with the wicked in this world.
And "Of laughter I said: it is praiseworthy" —

phrases.aramaic: זֶה שְׂחוֹק שֶׁמְּשַׂחֵק הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
phrases.english: this is the laughter that the Holy One, Blessed be He, laughs
with the righteous in the World to Come.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the first contradiction listed.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different situations: each verse refers to a different kind of laughter.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both verses talk about the same laughter, one praising it and one condemning it.
steps.terutzMaskana: Anger toward צדיקים in this world beats 'laughter' with רשעים in this world, and the praised laughter is with צדיקים in עולם הבא.

steps.title: Two kinds of joy: מצוה joy and empty joy
steps.stepSummary: The verse praising joy means שמחה של מצוה. The verse asking 'what does joy accomplish?' means joy that has nothing to do with a מצוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And I praised joy' means the joy of a מצוה. 'And of joy, what does it accomplish?' means joy that is not the joy of a מצוה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now solves the second contradiction from step 16, the one about joy. The two verses are describing two different kinds of joy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: קהלת both praises joy and seems to put it down. The answer splits joy into two types. Joy that comes from doing a מצוה is praised, and empty, pointless joy is the kind קהלת dismisses. With this, both verses are true.

keyTerms.meaning: Joy that comes from doing a מצוה

phrases.english: "And I praised joy"
this is the joy of a מצוה.
"And of joy, what does it accomplish?"
this is joy that is not of a מצוה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallels step 17. Step 17 solved the laughter contradiction, and this step solves the joy contradiction.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing two different types of the same thing (מצוה joy versus empty joy)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both verses talk about the same joy, so קהלת contradicts himself.
steps.terutzMaskana: Praised joy is שמחה של מצוה, and dismissed joy is joy without a מצוה.

steps.title: The שכינה rests only on a person in מצוה joy
steps.stepSummary: The verse comes to teach that the שכינה does not rest on a person who is sad, lazy, laughing, light-headed, chatting or idle. It rests only on a person in שמחה של מצוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: This teaches you that the שכינה does not rest on a person out of sadness, laziness, laughter, light-headedness, chatter or idle talk. It rests only out of the joy of a מצוה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a big lesson from the praise of מצוה joy. Only that kind of joy brings the שכינה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The list rules out two opposite mistakes. One is being too heavy, which means sadness and laziness. The other is being too light, which means laughter, light-headedness and empty talk. The right state is a joyful, serious closeness to מצוות.
steps.whatToRemember: The שכינה comes neither through gloom nor through silliness. It comes only through שמחה של מצוה.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a basic source in עבודת ה׳ for the idea that מצוה joy is a requirement for closeness to ה׳.

phrases.english: to teach you that the Divine Presence does not rest
not out of sadness,
and not out of laziness,
and not out of laughter,
and not out of frivolity,
and not out of idle conversation,
and not out of empty chatter,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא מִתּוֹךְ דְּבַר שִׂמְחָה שֶׁל מִצְוָה,
phrases.english: but only out of the joy of a מצוה,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a general lesson from the answer in step 18.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The שכינה rests on a person only through שמחה של מצוה.

steps.title: Proof from אלישע and the musician
steps.stepSummary: The verse about אלישע shows that the spirit of prophecy came back to him only after a musician played and brought him joy.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'Now bring me a musician. And when the musician played, the hand of ה׳ came upon him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק to prove that the שכינה comes through joy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אלישע had become angry, and his prophecy left him. He asked for music to bring back his joy, and only then did the hand of ה׳ return. This shows in practice that joy brings the שכינה.

keyTerms.meaning: The hand of ה׳, meaning prophecy

phrases.english: as it is stated: "But now bring me a musician;
and it came to pass, when the musician played,
that the hand of the Lord came upon him."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the scriptural proof for the lesson in step 19.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that the שכינה rests only through joy
steps.raayaSupportSource: מלכים ב 3:15. אלישע's prophecy returned when music brought him joy.

steps.title: רב יהודה: the same applies to teaching הלכה
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה says that one should also begin a matter of הלכה with joy.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: The same is true for a matter of הלכה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה extends the rule about joy to Torah learning. One should start teaching הלכה in a joyful mood.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Joy brings the שכינה, and it also helps Torah to be learned and said clearly. This statement becomes the target of the next challenge.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: וְכֵן לִדְבַר הֲלָכָה.
phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said: And so too for a matter of halakha.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: וְכֵן לִדְבַר הֲלָכָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the joy principle to Torah study.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One should approach a matter of הלכה with joy.

steps.title: רבא: the same applies to a good dream
steps.stepSummary: רבא says that going to sleep in joy leads to a good dream.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: The same is true for a good dream.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא adds one more place where joy helps. Going to sleep happy brings good dreams.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Dreams are seen as a small window to heavenly messages. So the joy rule applies to them too, just as it applies to prophecy.

phrases.english: Rava said: And so too for a good dream.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second extension of the joy principle, parallel to רב יהודה's.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One should go to sleep in a joyful state in order to have a good dream.

steps.title: Challenge: a student's lips must drip bitterness
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב יהודה from רב. According to רב, a תלמיד חכם sitting before his rebbe must have lips that 'drip bitterness,' meaning fear and awe, and not joy.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But רב גידל said in the name of רב: Any תלמיד חכם who sits before his rebbe and whose lips do not drip with bitterness, his lips should be burned. As it says: 'His lips are lilies, dripping flowing myrrh.' Do not read 'flowing myrrh' (מור עובר) but 'flowing bitterness' (מר עובר). Do not read 'lilies' (שושנים) but 'those who learn' (ששונים).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב יהודה's statement. Torah learning seems to need fear and seriousness, not joy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב reads a פסוק in a new way to teach that lips that learn Torah must drip 'bitterness,' meaning awe of the rebbe. That seems to clash directly with רב יהודה's rule to begin הלכה with joy.

keyTerms.meaning: Do not read [it this way], but read [it this way]

steps.confusionAlert: 'Do not read X, rather Y' does not change the פסוק. It adds an extra drasha layer of meaning on top of the plain reading.

phrases.aramaic: אִינִי, וְהָאָמַר רַב גִּידֵּל אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Is that so? But didn't Rav Giddel say that Rav said:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל תַּלְמִיד חָכָם שֶׁיּוֹשֵׁב לִפְנֵי רַבּוֹ
phrases.english: Any Torah scholar who sits before his teacher
and his lips do not drip bitterness, they shall be burnt,
as it is stated: "His lips are lilies, dripping flowing myrrh":
Do not read "flowing myrrh" but "flowing bitterness."
Do not read "lilies" but "that are learning."

steps.triggerLanguage: אִינִי, וְהָאָמַר רַב גִּידֵּל אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב יהודה's rule from step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's statement that one should approach הלכה with joy
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב requires bitterness and awe on the lips of one learning Torah before his rebbe, which is the opposite of joy.

steps.title: Answer 1: the rebbe is joyful, the student is in awe
steps.stepSummary: Joy applies to the rebbe who teaches. Bitterness and awe apply to the student who listens.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This one is about the rebbe, and that one is about the student.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by splitting the two statements between two different people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יהודה's joy is for the teacher, who should open the lesson happily. רב's bitterness is for the student, who must sit before his rebbe with fear. Each statement is talking about a different person.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this refers to a teacher, and that refers to a student.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא בְּרַבָּה וְהָא בְּתַלְמִידָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 23.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both statements are about the same person, so they clash.
steps.terutzMaskana: The teacher should be joyful, and the student should be in awe.

steps.title: Answer 2: both are about the rebbe, before and after he starts
steps.stepSummary: Alternatively, both statements are about the rebbe. He is joyful before he begins teaching and serious once he has begun.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you could say both are about the rebbe, and it is not difficult. This one is before he begins, and that one is after he has begun.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second way to answer. This time it splits the two statements by time instead of by person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this answer, even the rebbe moves from joy to awe. He opens with joy to prepare everyone, and once the הלכה itself starts, he becomes serious.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say (introduces an alternative answer)

phrases.english: And if you wish, say both this and that refer to a teacher,
and it is not difficult:
this is before he begins,
that is after he has begun.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to the same challenge, given in place of step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different stages in time (before versus during the lesson)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The teacher must be either joyful or serious the whole time.
steps.terutzMaskana: The teacher opens with joy and then teaches with awe.

steps.title: רבה's practice: a joke first, then awe
steps.stepSummary: רבה used to say something funny before teaching so the Sages would cheer up. Then he sat in awe and began the lesson.
steps.simpleTranslation: Like רבה: before he began teaching the Sages, he would say something funny and the Sages would be cheered. Then he would sit in awe and begin the lesson.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows a real example of the second answer in practice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה's routine matches answer 2 exactly. He used joy before starting, and awe once the actual שמעתא began. This shows the answer is how great teachers really acted.
steps.whatToRemember: A good rebbe opens with light joy and then teaches with serious awe.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הָא דְּרַבָּה מִקַּמֵּי דְּפָתַח לְהוּ לְרַבָּנַן
phrases.english: Like Rabba, who before he began teaching the Sages
would say something humorous
and the Sages would be cheered;
in the end he sat in awe
and began the lesson.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הָא דְּרַבָּה מִקַּמֵּי דְּפָתַח לְהוּ לְרַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates and supports the second answer in step 25.
steps.raayaObject: The second answer: joy before beginning, awe after beginning
steps.raayaSupportSource: The actual practice of רבה with his students

steps.title: חכמים also wanted to hide ספר משלי
steps.stepSummary: Like קהלת, the Sages wanted to put away ספר משלי because its statements seem to contradict each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: And they also wanted to hide away ספר משלי, because its statements contradict each other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new book. It reports that ספר משלי faced the same danger as קהלת, and this sets up the next questions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'also' (ואף) links this to the earlier discussion about hiding קהלת. The problem is the same, since a holy book seems to contradict itself.

keyTerms.meaning: To hide away, to remove from public use

phrases.english: And they sought to hide away the book of Proverbs as well,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁהָיוּ דְּבָרָיו סוֹתְרִין זֶה אֶת זֶה.
phrases.english: because its statements contradict each other.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a parallel discussion to the earlier one about קהלת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The Sages considered hiding ספר משלי because of its internal contradictions.

steps.title: Why didn't they hide it?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what stopped the Sages from hiding ספר משלי.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why didn't they hide it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a simple question. If the problem was real, what saved the book?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question sets up the reasoning in the next step.

phrases.english: And why did they not hide it away?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks a follow-up question about step 27.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What reason saved ספר משלי from being hidden

steps.title: Just as קהלת was explained, so can משלי be
steps.stepSummary: The Sages reasoned that they had studied קהלת and found explanations, so they should study משלי the same way.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: With ספר קהלת, didn't we look into it and find a reason? Here too, let us look into it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers. The success with קהלת showed that contradictions can be solved, so they tried the same with משלי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reasoning works from a past example. A contradiction that only seems to be there is not a reason to hide a holy book, as long as careful study can solve it.

phrases.english: They said: The book of Ecclesiastes, didn't we examine it
and find an explanation?
Here too, let us examine it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 28.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Because קהלת's contradictions were solved through study, they expected משלי's could be solved too.

steps.title: What exactly is the contradiction in משלי?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which statements in משלי contradict each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is the contradiction between its statements?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the actual example of the contradiction. This sets up the two verses that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before solving the problem, the גמרא has to show it clearly.

phrases.aramaic: וּמַאי דְּבָרָיו סוֹתְרִים זֶה אֶת זֶה?
phrases.english: And what is: its statements contradict each other?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַאי דְּבָרָיו סוֹתְרִים זֶה אֶת זֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the specific details behind the claim in step 27.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The specific verses in משלי that clash

steps.title: Don't answer a fool, and do answer a fool
steps.stepSummary: One פסוק says not to answer a fool according to his foolishness. The very next פסוק says to answer him.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is written: 'Do not answer a fool according to his foolishness.' And it is written: 'Answer a fool according to his foolishness.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows the contradiction. Two verses right next to each other give opposite instructions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: משלי 26:4 says not to answer, and 26:5 says to answer. At first glance it looks impossible to keep both.

phrases.english: It is written: "Answer not a fool according to his folly,"
and it is written: "Answer a fool according to his folly."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 30 by naming the contradiction.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: משלי 26:4 and 26:5 contradict each other about answering a fool.

steps.title: Torah matters versus everyday matters
steps.stepSummary: When a fool speaks about דברי תורה, answer him. When he speaks about everyday matters, do not.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This one is about דברי תורה, and that one is about worldly matters.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא solves the contradiction by assigning each verse to a different kind of topic.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a fool twists the Torah, one must answer him so that he does not think he is right. In everyday arguments, it is better to stay silent and not sink to his level. This saves ספר משלי.
steps.whatToRemember: Answer a fool who twists Torah. Ignore a fool in everyday matters.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this is regarding Torah matters,
that is regarding worldly matters.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction shown in step 31.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different subject matter (Torah versus everyday topics)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both verses speak about the same kind of conversation, so they contradict.
steps.terutzMaskana: Answer the fool in Torah matters, and do not answer him in everyday matters.

steps.title: The fool who insulted רבי
steps.stepSummary: A man came to רבי and claimed that רבי's wife was his wife and רבי's children were his children. רבי offered him a cup of wine, and he drank it and burst.
steps.simpleTranslation: Like the man who came before רבי and said: Your wife is my wife, and your children are my children. רבי said to him: Would you like to drink a cup of wine? He drank and burst.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא illustrates the 'everyday matters' half of the rule in step 32: when a fool makes a brazen claim that is not about Torah, the Sage does not answer him with argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man's claim was an attack that would have made רבי's children ממזרים. רבי did not argue with him, and the man died on the spot. Step 35 will explain why.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הָא דְּהָהוּא דַּאֲתָא לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי
phrases.english: Like that man who came before Rabbi
and said to him: Your wife is my wife,
and your children are my children.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: רְצוֹנֶךָ שֶׁתִּשְׁתֶּה כּוֹס שֶׁל יַיִן?
phrases.english: He said to him: Would you like to drink a cup of wine?
He drank and burst.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הָא דְּהָהוּא דַּאֲתָא לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates the rule about dealing with a fool from step 32.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that one does not answer a fool in everyday (non-Torah) matters

steps.title: The fool who insulted רבי חייא
steps.stepSummary: A man told רבי חייא that רבי חייא's mother was his wife and that רבי חייא was his son. He was offered wine, drank, and burst.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man came before רבי חייא and said to him: Your mother is my wife, and you are my son. He said to him: Would you like to drink a cup of wine? He drank and burst.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second, very similar story involving רבי חייא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This time the insult aimed at רבי חייא's own lineage. The ending is the same, and the brazen man was punished from Heaven.

phrases.english: That man who came before Rabbi Ḥiyya

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִמְּךָ אִשְׁתִּי, וְאַתָּה בְּנִי.
phrases.english: said to him: Your mother is my wife, and you are my son.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: רְצוֹנֶךָ שֶׁתִּשְׁתֶּה כּוֹס שֶׁל יַיִן?
phrases.english: He said to him: Would you like to drink a cup of wine?
He drank and burst.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel second story to step 33.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that one does not answer a fool in everyday (non-Torah) matters

steps.title: רבי's prayer protected his children
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא explains that רבי's daily prayer to be saved from עזי פנים is what protected רבי's children from being labeled ממזרים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא said: רבי's prayer helped him so that his children would not be made ממזרים. For when רבי prayed, he would say: 'May it be Your will, ה׳ our God, that You save me today from brazen people and from brazenness.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חייא gives the reason behind the first story. רבי's prayer is what stopped the brazen man.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי prayed every day to be protected from עזי פנים. When a brazen man tried to slander his family, the prayer worked and the man died before his claim could do harm. This prayer is still said today in ברכות השחר.

keyTerms.meaning: It helped him, it was effective for him

steps.whatToRemember: רבי's prayer against עזי פנים, which we still say every morning, protected his family from slander.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the יהי רצון in ברכות השחר asking to be saved from עזי פנים.

phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥiyya said:
Rabbi's prayer was effective for him
so that his children were not made mamzerim.
For when Rabbi would pray, he said:
"May it be Your will, Lord our God,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁתַּצִּילֵנִי הַיּוֹם מֵעַזֵּי פָּנִים וּמֵעַזּוּת פָּנִים״.
phrases.english: that You save me today from brazen people and from brazenness."

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא: אַהְנְיָא לֵיהּ צְלוֹתֵיהּ לְרַבִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the cause behind the outcome of the story in step 33.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי's daily prayer against עזי פנים protected his children from being declared ממזרים.

steps.title: What does answering a fool in Torah matters look like?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a real example of answering a fool when he speaks about דברי תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: In דברי תורה, what is an example of this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a concrete case of the rule from Step 32, that you answer a fool when he speaks about Torah. This question sets up the stories that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 32 split the two פסוקים into Torah matters and everyday matters. Now the גמרא wants to see the Torah side in action. This tells us what the right kind of answer looks like.

keyTerms.meaning: What is it? (asks for an example)

phrases.english: In Torah matters, what is it?
phrases.notes: Refers back to the rule that you answer a fool in Torah matters.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the rule of Step 32 after the stories about רבי and רבי חייא, and asks for an example of its Torah side.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A real case showing how one answers a fool in Torah matters.

steps.title: A woman giving birth every day, and the hen
steps.stepSummary: רבן גמליאל teaches that in the future a woman will give birth every day. A student mocks him, and he shows him a hen as an example.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן גמליאל was sitting and teaching: In the future a woman will give birth every day, as the פסוק says 'pregnant and giving birth together.' A student mocked him and said: 'There is nothing new under the sun!' רבן גמליאל said: Come and I will show you an example in this world. He went out and showed him a hen.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question with a story. רבן גמליאל answers a mocking student by showing him something real in this world, a hen that lays an egg every day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The student uses a פסוק to attack the teaching, so this is a fool speaking about Torah. רבן גמליאל does not ignore him. He answers by showing that something like this already exists in nature, so it is not completely 'new.'

keyTerms.meaning: Was expounding or teaching a פסוק
In the future (the World to Come)

steps.confusionAlert: רבן גמליאל is not saying that a hen gives birth to live chicks every day. The point is that a hen produces an egg daily. That is a 'birth' in a sense, so the idea is not foreign to this world.

phrases.english: Like this: Rabban Gamliel was sitting
and expounding:
In the future, a woman will give birth every day,
as it says: 'pregnant and giving birth together.'
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 31. He reads it to mean she conceives and gives birth on the same day.

phrases.english: A certain student mocked him,
and said: 'There is nothing new under the sun'!
He said to him: Come and I will show you
an example of them in this world.
He went out and showed him a hen.
phrases.notes: A hen lays an egg every day.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הָא דְּיָתֵיב רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל וְקָא דָרֵישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 36 with a story.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: When a student mocks a Torah teaching, you answer him. רבן גמליאל did this by showing the student a hen.

steps.title: Trees giving fruit every day, and the caper bush
steps.stepSummary: A second story: רבן גמליאל teaches that trees will give fruit daily. The student mocks him again, and he shows him a caper bush.
steps.simpleTranslation: Also: רבן גמליאל taught that in the future trees will produce fruit every day, as the פסוק says 'it will bring forth branches and make fruit.' Just as branches grow every day, fruit will grow every day. The student mocked him: 'But it is written: There is nothing new under the sun!' He said: Come and I will show you an example in this world. He went out and showed him a caper bush.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second story with the same pattern: a teaching, the student's mocking, and a real-world example.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here רבן גמליאל uses a comparison: fruit is placed next to branches, which grow daily, so fruit will also grow daily. The caper bush has some edible part in every season, so it shows that constant fruit-bearing already exists.

phrases.english: And furthermore: Rabban Gamliel sat and expounded:

phrases.english: In the future, trees will produce fruit every day,
as it says: 'It will bring forth branches and make fruit,'

phrases.english: just as a branch grows every day, so too fruit every day.
A certain student mocked him,

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר: וְהָכְתִיב ״אֵין כׇּל חָדָשׁ תַּחַת הַשָּׁמֶשׁ״.

He said to him: Come and I will show you
an example of them in this world.
He went out and showed him a caper bush.
phrases.notes: Some part of it is edible in every season.

steps.title: The land producing cakes and fine garments, and the mushrooms
steps.stepSummary: A third story: רבן גמליאל teaches that ארץ ישראל will produce baked cakes and fine wool clothing. He shows the student truffles and mushrooms, and the covering of a young palm shoot.
steps.simpleTranslation: Also: רבן גמליאל taught that in the future ארץ ישראל will produce cakes and fine wool garments, as the פסוק says 'Let there be abundant grain in the land.' The student mocked him: 'There is nothing new under the sun.' He said: Come and I will show you an example in this world. He went out and showed him truffles and mushrooms. For the fine garments, he showed him the soft covering of a young palm shoot.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third and final story of the same kind. This time רבן גמליאל gives two examples, one for the food and one for the clothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Truffles and mushrooms pop out of the ground overnight, already ready to eat, much like a baked loaf growing from the earth. The fiber wrapped around a young palm shoot looks like woven cloth, so clothing growing from the ground also has an example in this world.

keyTerms.meaning: The fibrous covering of a young palm shoot

steps.whatToRemember: All three stories follow one pattern: a teaching about the future, a student mocking with 'nothing new under the sun,' and a real-world example. This is what answering a fool in דברי תורה looks like.

phrases.aramaic: וְתוּ, יָתֵיב רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל וְקָא דָרֵישׁ:
phrases.english: And furthermore: Rabban Gamliel sat and expounded:
In the future, the Land of Israel will produce
cakes and fine wool garments,
as it says: 'Let there be abundant grain in the land.'
A certain student mocked him and said:
'There is nothing new under the sun.'
He said to him: Come and I will show you
an example of them in this world.
He went out and showed him truffles and mushrooms.
phrases.notes: They spring up overnight, ready to eat, like bread.

phrases.english: And for the fine wool garments: the covering of a young palm shoot.
phrases.notes: A thin, cloth-like covering that grows naturally.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתוּ, יָתֵיב רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל וְקָא דָרֵישׁ: עֲתִידָה אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a third story of the same pattern and closes the series.
steps.raayaObject: How to answer a fool in Torah matters

steps.title: Be patient like הלל, not strict like שמאי
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that a person should always be humble and patient like הלל, and not quick to become upset like שמאי.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: A person should always be humble and patient like הלל, and not strict and impatient like שמאי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic, a ברייתא about patience. It connects to the earlier theme of how חכמים respond to foolish or provoking people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The stories above showed חכמים responding calmly to mockery. Now the גמרא brings a general rule of good character: be like הלל, who stayed patient, and not like שמאי, who was strict. Stories proving this rule follow.
steps.whyThisMatters: This ברייתא opens the famous stories about הלל's patience that follow on the daf.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
A person should always be humble and patient like Hillel
and not strict like Shammai.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: לְעוֹלָם יְהֵא אָדָם עַנְוְותָן כְּהִלֵּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shifts from answering fools to the related theme of patience with provoking people.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person should always be patient like הלל and not strict like שמאי.

steps.title: Opening of the story of the two men
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא begins a story about two people. This story will show הלל's patience.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was an incident with two people...
steps.whatsHappening: This line opens a story that will illustrate the rule just stated. It sets up the next move, and the story continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word מעשה signals that a real event is coming to support the rule of Step 40. So far only the characters, two people, are introduced.

phrases.english: There was an incident with two people
phrases.notes: The story continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a story to support the ברייתא of Step 40.
